study.title: Revelation 21 The holy city, the presence of God, and the final separation
study.overview: Revelation 21 contains the great Christian hope with two images connected: the total renewal of creation and the descent of the new Jerusalem. The chapter shows that consummation is not only the escape of this world, but the formation by God of a new, holy and inhabited reality by it. The city is presented as a bride, which highlights purity, covenant and bridal joy between God and his people. At the same time, the text affirms a solemn exclusion: nothing unclean enters into this city, and only those inscribed in the Lamb's book of life remain in it.

outline.title: New creation and the comforting presence of God
outline.explanation: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, a sign that the old order passed. The new Jerusalem descends from God as a city prepared for the bridegroom, and the divine voice proclaims full dwelling with human beings, the end of death and pain, and renewal of all things.

outline.title: Completion of the promise and contrast between inheritance and judgment
outline.explanation: God declares the finished work, identifies himself as the beginning and the end, and offers free water of life. The victors receive inheritance and sonship, while those who persist in unbelief and uncleanness are destined for the lake of fire, called second death.

outline.title: The city-novest in glory, order and beauty
outline.explanation: An angel shows John the new Jerusalem as the bride of the Lamb. The description highlights the glory of God, the doors with the names of the tribes, the foundations with the names of the apostles, perfect measures and precious materials, emphasizing holiness, order and incomparable value.

outline.title: God and the Lamb as light and temple; the city without contamination
outline.explanation: There is no separate temple, because the Lord God himself and the Lamb are the temple and the light of the city. The nations bring their honor to her, the doors never close, but nothing defiled enters it; only the writings in the Lamb's book of life remain there.

study.context: The chapter is part of the final vision of the Apocalypse and, in the given notes, is presented as a picture of the future consummation of God's people. Tyndale notes that these scenes strengthen persecuted Christians. The notes also record a reading that understands the new Jerusalem as a holy and pure community, in contrast to Babylon. Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke mention that many interpreters see here the perfect and triumphant condition of the church in the final state, often understood as celestial reality.
study.theology: The theological center of the chapter is God's immediate presence with his people. Salvation ends not only in forgiveness, but in consummated communion: God dwells with human beings, wipes out every tear and eliminates death. The new creation is the gift of God, not human conquest. The language of the bride shows that the city is also people, belonging and alliance. The text maintains union between promise and judgment: the same grace that invites the water of life establishes a moral and spiritual frontier, in which impurity, lies and idolatry are incompatible with the holy city. The entrance is defined by the inscription in the book of the life of the Lamb, which points to dependence on the redeemer and not to human merit.

scholarViews.insight: The new Jerusalem is presented as the bride, that is, all who respond to the message of Christ's salvation; the picture contrasts with Babylon as a whore.
The vision of the new heavens and the new earth is more surely understood as a representation of the perfect and triumphant heavenly state of God's people.
Nothing contaminated enters the city; this exclusion reaches both moral impurity and doctrinal falsehood, and only those inscribed in the book of life enter.

questions: How does the promise that God inhabits with his own must change the way we face suffering and death today?
What contrast does the chapter establish between the Bride city and Babylon, and what does this teach about spiritual purity?
If the entrance to the city depends on the Lamb's book of life, how does this correct a trust in human merits?
study.practice: Long live Christian hope as consolation and holiness. In times of pain, remember that God promises an end to tears and renewal of all things. In times of temptation, treat seriously the warning that lies, idolatry and uncleanness do not match the holy city. Cultivate a persevering faith, asking God to align his life with the future reality he himself prepares.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided admit that some images can be read more literally or more symbolically, especially the new Jerusalem, the measures of the city, and the relationship between the vision and the church or the heavenly final state. The text and notes do not allow for sure geographical, chronological or architectural details beyond what was explicitly said.
